sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
Convexity changes what a stationary point is worth. For a general smooth function, a zero gradient is only a candidate. For a differentiable convex function, the graph lies above every tangent. At a point where the gradient vanishes, the tangent is the horizontal line at the function value, so every other point of the domain lies on or above that line. The stationary point is a global minimizer.

The same conclusion can be reached from the local side. A local minimizer of a convex function is global, with or without a derivative. Differentiability adds the convenient test: find a stationary point, and you are done. There is no second valley hiding somewhere else.

Strict convexity adds uniqueness. If two distinct points shared the minimum value, the chord between them would lie on the graph, and strict convexity forbids that. A strictly convex differentiable function has at most one stationary point, and if it has one, that point is the unique global minimizer. A convex function that is not strict can have a whole line of minimizers, as a square of a single linear form does.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
If \(f\) is differentiable and convex and \(\nabla f(x^\star) = 0\), then \(f(y) \ge f(x^\star)\) for every \(y\) in the domain. The reason is the tangent inequality
\[
f(y) \ge f(x^\star) + \nabla f(x^\star)^T (y - x^\star) = f(x^\star).
\]
If \(f\) is strictly convex, the minimizer is unique. A positive definite Hessian everywhere implies strict convexity. A positive semidefinite Hessian everywhere implies convexity and allows a nontrivial argmin set.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(f(t) = 2t^2 - 8t + 23\). The derivative is \(4t - 8\), which vanishes at \(t = 2\). The second derivative is the positive constant 4, so \(f\) is strictly convex and the stationary point is the unique global minimizer. The convex floor is 15, because \(f(2) = 8 - 16 + 23\).

Completing the square tells the same story: \(f(t) = 2(t - 2)^2 + 15\). The constant 23 moved the floor and did not move the minimizer. If the leading coefficient were zero, the function would be affine, still convex, and a stationary point would exist only in the degenerate case of a zero slope, where every point is a minimizer.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The convexity hypothesis is not optional. The derivative of \(t^3\) vanishes at the origin, and \(t^3\) is not convex, and the origin is not a minimizer. Quoting the theorem without the hypothesis is the usual false proof. A second mistake is to expect uniqueness from convexity alone. The function \(x^2\) on the plane is convex, stationary on the whole second axis, and every one of those points is a global minimizer. Strict convexity is the extra ingredient. A positive definite Hessian at a single point does not make the function convex on its domain.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A positive definite quadratic is the cleanest case: one linear system, one solution, and a theorem that says the solution is the unique global minimizer. On a convex feasible set the zero-gradient test is replaced by a variational inequality, and convexity of the objective again promotes that first-order condition to global optimality. Least squares is a convex quadratic, so the normal equations are enough.
